title: Socrates' last day
hookLine: Athens, 399 BCE: he spends his final hours talking with friends about the soul (Plato, Phaedo)
tomorrow: I know that I don't know

lines: IF IT WERE YOUR LAST DAY.
cards: If you knew it was your last day, how would you spend it? People answer fast at parties: a beach, a big meal, calling everyone you love. In Athens, a man past seventy actually knew.
And he spent it doing exactly what he'd done every other day of his life: talking with his friends, and asking questions.
He opens a new week, a week of ordinary saints: not kings or prophets, just people who lived their questions all the way through.

teach.h: THE TRIAL AND THE SACRED SHIP.
teach.b: Socrates had been put on trial by his own city, charged with not honoring the city's gods and with corrupting the young. A jury of Athenians found him guilty and sentenced him to death.
But a sacred ship had just sailed to the island of Delos, and by custom no one could be executed until it came back. So he waited in prison a long while, and his friends came every day.

teach.h: PLATO WASN'T THERE; HE WAS ILL.
teach.b: His student Plato wrote about the last of those days in the Phaedo, told in the voice of a friend who was there. And Plato lets that friend mention, in passing, that Plato himself was absent: ill, he believes.
So it's a story written by a friend, about what other friends saw. That morning the chains come off.
Socrates rubs his leg and remarks how pleasure and pain seem joined together; Aesop, he adds, could have made a fable of it. He'd even been turning Aesop's fables into verse in his cell.
Then, all day, he talks with his friends about the soul, and whether it survives death.

teach.h: A LAST DAY OF HARD QUESTIONS.
teach.b: Two of them, Simmias and Cebes, raise hard objections, and Socrates doesn't get defensive. He welcomes them. Don't agree with me to be kind, he tells them, more or less; follow the argument.

At sunset he bathes, says goodbye to his family, and calmly drinks the poison the city has prepared. His last words are a small, strange request to his friend Crito: to pay a debt, a rooster owed to the god of healing.
People still argue about what that meant. What stays is the picture: with hours left, he wasn't settling things.
He was still asking, and still glad to be asked.

how: Students of philosophy often meet Socrates in the Phaedo, and his calm, questioning last day is often held up as a picture of facing death with a clear mind.

o: a Greek king who ruled Athens at its height
a Roman poet who wrote fables about animals
an Athenian who spent his life asking questions

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: wrote it, but was ill that day

s: Plato was at Socrates' side at the end
in the Phaedo, the narrator says Plato was ill and not there.
Socrates had been putting Aesop's fables into verse in prison
and he joked that Aesop could have made a fable of pleasure and pain.
Socrates asked his friends to agree with him
he welcomed their objections and told them to follow the argument.

games.q: you're Socrates, with one day left. your friends Simmias and Cebes start picking holes in your argument about the soul. what do you do?
o: ask them to let you have your last day in peace
welcome the objections and keep reasoning
change the subject to lighter things
games.why: he welcomes them and keeps reasoning with them all day. he asks them to follow the argument, not to agree with him out of kindness.

practice: Think of someone you'll probably talk to soon, not the easiest person and not the hardest, and one real question you could ask them: not about logistics, but what they think, or what they've been wondering lately.
Picture asking it, and listening to the answer without rushing to agree or correct. Socrates' friends disagreed with him on his last day, and he was glad.

wordCard.voice: Socrates. A whole final day spent in conversation about the soul, welcoming hard questions, until the sunset.

orig.note: Greek: psyche, soul. what Socrates and his friends talked about all day.

carryVoice: Your line: keep asking. His very last day was a day of questions. Until tomorrow.
